code.title: repr vs str: fallback and containers
code.python:
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x, self.y = x, y

    def __repr__(self):
        # developer view: unambiguous, !r keeps quotes on strings
        return f"Point(x={self.x!r}, y={self.y!r})"


class Tag(Point):
    def __str__(self):
        # user view: readable; used by print() and str()
        return f"<{self.x},{self.y}>"


p = Point(1, "two")
print("print(p)      :", p)        # no __str__, falls back to __repr__
print("repr(p)       :", repr(p))
t = Tag(3, 4)
print("print(t)      :", t)        # uses __str__
print("repr(t)       :", repr(t))
print("f'{t}' / !r   :", f"{t}", f"{t!r}")
print("list of tags  :", [t])      # containers always use repr

followUps:
It stops repr from recursing forever when an object contains itself. Without a guard, a list that holds itself would call repr on itself endlessly.

@recursive_repr() wraps your __repr__, remembers which objects are being printed (per thread), and returns '...' when it meets one a second time. Example: a = []; a.append(a) prints [[...]]. Cost is a small set lookup per call.

format(obj, spec) calls obj.__format__(spec), and an f-string f"{obj:spec}" passes the text after the colon as that spec. The default object.__format__ accepts only an empty spec and then returns str(obj); any other spec raises TypeError.

Override it for custom specs: f"{temp:.1f}" can be handled by forwarding to format(self.value, spec). !r and !s convert first, then format.

code.title: Truthiness: __bool__, then __len__

followUps:
NumPy refuses because an array of many elements has no single sensible truth value: should [0, 1] be true because one item is, or false because one is not? Guessing would hide bugs, so __bool__ raises ValueError for arrays longer than one element.

Ask the question you mean: a.any(), a.all(), or a.size == 0. Example: if arr == 3: builds a boolean array first, which is why the error appears there. Chained comparisons and and trigger it too.

It must return a non-negative int (anything with __index__ works). Returning a float or a negative number raises TypeError or ValueError, so len(x) is always a count you can trust.

The value is also limited to sys.maxsize (about 9.2 quintillion on 64-bit), otherwise OverflowError. Example: def __len__(self): return 2.5 fails with 'float' object cannot be interpreted as an integer. __bool__, by contrast, must return exactly True or False.

code.title: Broken vs correct __eq__/__hash__

followUps:
Because Python defines numeric equality across types: 1 == 1.0 == True is True, so the contract forces their hashes to match. Otherwise a dict would hold both 1 and 1.0 as separate keys.

Integers hash to themselves (modulo a large prime), floats with whole values hash like that int, and True is just 1. Example: d = {1: 'a'}; d[1.0] gives 'a', and {1, 1.0, True} has one element. Your own numeric-like class should follow the same rule.

unsafe_hash=True makes the dataclass generate __hash__ from its fields even though the class stays mutable. It is acceptable only when you promise never to change those fields while the object is in a set or dict.

Without it, eq=True and not frozen means __hash__ = None. Prefer frozen=True, which makes the hash safe by blocking assignment. Example use: a mutable config you hash briefly as a cache key, then discard. Exclude volatile fields with field(hash=False) or compare=False.

code.title: NotImplemented lets the other operand try

followUps:
Nothing useful: the NotImplementedError class is a truthy object, so a == b would quietly return that exception object as the result and if a == b: would take the true branch. No error is raised and the wrong answer spreads.

For arithmetic you would get a weird value instead of a TypeError. Always check the spelling: the singleton is NotImplemented; the exception NotImplementedError belongs in abstract methods you raise, never return. Linters such as pylint flag this mistake.

Fraction builds each operator from a forward and a reverse function made by one helper, _operator_fallbacks. The forward function handles Fraction and int exactly, converts to float or complex when the other side is one, and otherwise returns NotImplemented.

So Fraction(1, 2) + 0.25 gives 0.75 (a float), and Fraction(1, 2) + 'x' falls through to TypeError. The reverse version covers 1 + Fraction(1, 2), where int says NotImplemented first.

code.title: How a + b is dispatched
code.python:
class A:
    def __add__(self, o):
        print("  A.__add__")
        return NotImplemented
    def __radd__(self, o):
        print("  A.__radd__")
        return "A.__radd__ result"


class B(A):
    def __radd__(self, o):           # subclass overrides the reflected method
        print("  B.__radd__")
        return "B.__radd__ result"


class C:
    def __radd__(self, o):
        print("  C.__radd__")
        return "C.__radd__ result"


print("A() + C():")
print(" ->", A() + C())              # A.__add__ declines, then C.__radd__
print("A() + B():  (B subclass of A, overrides __radd__)")
print(" ->", A() + B())              # right operand tried first
print("A() + 1:")
try:
    A() + 1
except TypeError as e:
    print(" -> TypeError:", e)

a = [1]
b = a
a += [2]                             # __iadd__ mutates in place
print("list +=  same object:", a is b, b)
x = (1,)
y = x
x += (2,)                            # no __iadd__: rebinds to a new tuple
print("tuple += same object:", x is y, y, x)

followUps:
sum() starts with the integer 0 and computes 0 + item, so the left operand is an int that knows nothing about your class. int.__add__ returns NotImplemented, and Python then calls item.__radd__(0).

Without __radd__, sum([Money(1), Money(2)]) raises TypeError. Fixes: define __radd__ to handle 0 (return self), or pass a start value: sum(items, Money(0)). The loop is O(N) additions.

The line both fails and succeeds: t = ([1],); t[0] += [2] raises TypeError, yet t becomes ([1, 2],).

Steps: read t[0] (the list), run list.__iadd__, which extends the list in place and returns it, then try t[0] = result. The tuple refuses item assignment, hence the error, but the in-place change already happened. Lesson: do not use += on a mutable item inside a tuple; call t[0].extend([2]) instead.

code.title: C3 linearization computed by hand

followUps:
Make it fail when the base list order contradicts the parents' own orders. class A: pass, class B(A): pass, then class X(A, B): pass raises TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order.

Why: L[B] = B A o demands B before A, but the base list [A, B] demands A before B. Merge finds A in the tail of [B A o] and B in the tail of [A, B], so no head qualifies. Fix by listing the more specific base first: X(B, A).

Depth-first search visits the shared parent before the second branch, so a method overridden in the sibling is skipped. For D(B, C) with both under A, classic order was D, B, A, C: A came before C.

If A defines save() and C overrides it, D().save() ran A's version and C's override was never reached, breaking the rule that children come before parents. C3 gives D, B, C, A, so C's override wins. New-style classes (Python 2.3+, all of Python 3) use C3.

code.title: Cooperative super() in a diamond

followUps:
Wrap it in a small adapter class that calls super().__init__() properly, or avoid inheritance and use composition. A non-cooperative class never forwards the call, so the chain stops at it.

Place it last in the bases so it ends the chain, and give the adapter the forwarding: class Adapter(Mixin, ThirdParty): def __init__(self, **kw): super().__init__(**kw). If it takes positional arguments you do not control, call ThirdParty.__init__(self, a, b) explicitly once, and have it be the last in the MRO so nothing after it is skipped.

It starts the search after C in the MRO of type(obj) and binds the found method to obj, so you can jump over classes on purpose. Example: with MRO D, B, C, A, super(C, d).m() looks at A first.

The two-argument form needs isinstance(obj, C), otherwise TypeError. Zero-argument super() is this call with the current class and self filled in. Given explicit arguments you pass them to the found method like any call: super(C, d).m(5) calls A's m(d, 5).

code.title: @property validation and pitfalls

followUps:
Cached_property computes once and stores the result in the instance __dict__, while property with lru_cache caches by self in a class-wide table. The first avoids extra memory per class and cleans up with the instance.

With lru_cache on a method, the cache holds a strong reference to every self, which can leak objects, requires self to be hashable, and is capped by maxsize. cached_property is a non-data descriptor, so after the first read the plain dict value wins and later reads cost one dict lookup; delete the attribute to reset it.

A descriptor lets one validator class guard many attributes. Define __set_name__ to learn the attribute name, __get__ and __set__ to read and check.

class Positive:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name): self.n = '_' + name
    def __get__(self, obj, t): return getattr(obj, self.n)
    def __set__(self, obj, v):
        if v <= 0: raise ValueError
        setattr(obj, self.n, v)

Use price = Positive() once per field instead of copying a property for each.

code.title: Attribute lookup order ladder
code.python:
class Data:                           # data descriptor: has __set__
    def __get__(self, obj, owner):
        return "from data descriptor"
    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        print("  Data.__set__ called")


class NonData:                        # non-data descriptor: only __get__
    def __get__(self, obj, owner):
        return "from non-data descriptor"


class Demo:
    d = Data()
    n = NonData()
    plain = "class attribute"

    def __getattr__(self, name):      # last resort
        return f"__getattr__({name})"


o = Demo()
o.__dict__["d"] = "instance d"
o.__dict__["n"] = "instance n"
o.__dict__["plain"] = "instance plain"
print("d     :", o.d)                 # data descriptor beats instance dict
print("n     :", o.n)                 # instance dict beats non-data descriptor
print("plain :", o.plain)             # instance dict beats class attribute
print("nope  :", o.nope)              # all steps failed, __getattr__ runs
print("assign o.d = 1:")
o.d = 1                               # goes to Data.__set__, not the dict
print("instance dict d still:", o.__dict__["d"])

followUps:
__getattribute__ runs for every attribute access; __getattr__ runs only when normal lookup has already failed with AttributeError.

So __getattr__ is safe for fallbacks (proxies, lazy values): def __getattr__(self, n): return self._data[n]. Overriding __getattribute__ is risky because even self._data goes through it and recurses; call super().__getattribute__(name) inside. It also slows every access, so use it only for logging or access control.

Operators and builtins such as len(x) or x + y skip the instance and __getattribute__ and go straight to the type's slot, while obj.name runs the full ladder.

Example: setting x.__len__ = f changes x.__len__() but not len(x). This is why a proxy with __getattr__ forwards px.append but fails len(px). Explicit dunder calls like x.__len__() do use the normal ladder; only implicit use is bypassed.

code.title: @dataclass generated features

followUps:
A dataclass rejects a list default because every instance would share the same list object, so one instance's change would show up in all others. This is the same trap as a mutable default argument in a function.

Dataclasses check at class creation and raise ValueError for list, dict and set defaults (any unhashable default). Use field(default_factory=list), which calls list() afresh for each new object. Immutable defaults like 0, 'x' or () are fine.

Pick by what you need: a dataclass for ordinary mutable records, a NamedTuple for light immutable records that behave like tuples, pydantic when data comes from outside and must be validated.

  • dataclass: no validation unless you write it, optional methods, can be frozen or slotted.
  • NamedTuple: immutable, unpackable, indexable, hashable, smallest.
  • pydantic: checks and converts types at runtime (third-party package, slower).

Example: a parsed JSON request goes to pydantic; a (x, y) point to a NamedTuple.

code.title: ABC vs Protocol vs register

followUps:
Subclassing dict is a trap because the C-level methods do not call your overrides. If you override __setitem__, then update(), setdefault() and the constructor dict(a=1) bypass it, so your validation is skipped.

Example: a Upper(dict) that uppercases keys in __setitem__ still stores 'a' after d.update(a=1). Safer: subclass collections.abc.MutableMapping (or UserDict) and implement 5 methods; every other method is built on them.

register() only makes isinstance and issubclass say yes. It does not check that the abstract methods exist, does not add inherited mixin methods, and does not put the ABC in the MRO.

Example: after Shape.register(Duck), isinstance(Duck(), Shape) is True, but Duck().describe() raises AttributeError and a missing area is never reported. Type checkers also do not see the relation. It is meant for third-party classes you cannot edit.

code.title: __slots__ removes the instance dict
code.python:
import sys


class Plain:
    def __init__(self):
        self.x, self.y, self.z = 1, 2, 3


class Slotted:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y", "z")       # fixed fields, no per-instance __dict__

    def __init__(self):
        self.x, self.y, self.z = 1, 2, 3


class SlottedChild(Slotted):
    pass                              # forgot __slots__: __dict__ comes back


p, s, c = Plain(), Slotted(), SlottedChild()
print("Plain has __dict__        :", hasattr(p, "__dict__"))
print("Slotted has __dict__      :", hasattr(s, "__dict__"))
print("SlottedChild has __dict__ :", hasattr(c, "__dict__"))
print("getsizeof Plain + dict    :", sys.getsizeof(p) + sys.getsizeof(p.__dict__) > sys.getsizeof(s))
try:
    s.w = 4                           # typos become errors
except AttributeError as e:
    print("AttributeError:", e)
try:
    s.__weakref__
except AttributeError:
    print("no __weakref__ unless you add it to __slots__")

N = 100_000
import tracemalloc
tracemalloc.start()
a = [Plain() for _ in range(N)]
m1 = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[0]
del a
b = [Slotted() for _ in range(N)]
m2 = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[0]
print("slotted smaller than plain:", m2 < m1)

followUps:
Measure with tracemalloc or by summing sys.getsizeof of the object plus its __dict__, not getsizeof of the object alone, because the dict is a separate allocation that a bare call hides.

Create 100,000 instances of each class in a fresh process, compare tracemalloc.get_traced_memory() before and after, and delete the first list before building the second. Compare peak memory too, and test with your real field count: savings grow with more attributes and shrink in newer CPython where instance dicts are leaner.

Leave objects behind when you hold millions of numeric records and run the same operation over all of them, since NumPy or pandas store values in packed arrays and loop in C.

Example: 1,000,000 points as slotted objects take roughly 50 to 60 MB and a Python loop to sum x; two float64 arrays take 16 MB and a.sum() runs in milliseconds. Keep slotted classes when you need behaviour per object, mixed types, or few thousand objects.

code.title: Dunders are looked up on the type

followUps:
MagicMock pre-creates the common dunders as class-level slots on a fresh subclass for each mock, so operators work. Plain Mock does not support them.

Each MagicMock instance gets its own subclass, and the supported methods (__len__, __iter__, __getitem__, __enter__ and others) are set on that class with sensible defaults: len(m) returns 0, bool(m) is True. You set values with m.__len__.return_value = 3. This works precisely because dunders live on the type.

None: operators and builtins never fall back to __getattr__ for dunders on new-style classes, so a proxy must define them itself. That is the lesson of the old-style behaviour, where an instance forwarded len(x) through __getattr__.

Only explicit calls like px.__len__() reach __getattr__. Example: len(Proxy([1])) raises TypeError. To forward, write the methods or generate them in a loop: for n in ('__len__', '__iter__'): setattr(Proxy, n, lambda s, *a, n=n: getattr(s._t, n)(*a)).
